passage: Newsrooms once knew remarkably little about their readers. An editor could see how many copies were sold, but not which articles were read, how far, or by whom; judgements about what the public wanted were made on instinct, on letters to the editor and on the preferences of the editor's own circle. Today a screen in the corner of the room can show, minute by minute, how many people are reading each story, and a headline can be tested in two versions on live audiences, the weaker one retired within the hour. Critics regard this as the moment journalism surrendered to the crowd. The charge deserves a more careful answer than either its proponents or its targets usually give.

The first thing to say is that the numbers are not lies. A click records a real decision, made by a real person, to open one article rather than another. What it records, however, is narrower than it appears. It measures the pull of a headline at the instant of choice, not the worth of what follows, and still less whether the reader was better informed for having read it. A story that disappoints everyone who opens it can outperform one that rewards every reader, provided its headline promises more. When a newsroom treats these figures as a verdict on its journalism, it is reading a measure of curiosity as if it were a measure of value. Curiosity matters, and a story that nobody opens informs nobody, but it is only one of the things a newspaper exists to serve.

The damage done by this misreading is gradual. No editor decides to abandon difficult subjects; it is only that, week after week, the stories that perform poorly on the screen are given less space, fewer reporters and less prominent positions, and the subjects they belong to slowly thin out. Each individual decision is defensible, since space is limited and something must give way, and that is precisely why the cumulative effect is so rarely noticed until it is well advanced. Coverage of committee hearings, foreign elections and the routine work of public agencies is especially vulnerable, not because readers have rejected it but because the measure in use was never designed to register its value.

It would be naive to conclude that newsrooms should switch the screens off. The instincts the screens replaced were not neutral; they reflected the tastes of a narrow group of editors, who often mistook their own interests for the public's. Some organisations now try to measure better things, such as how long readers stay, whether they return and whether they subscribe. These are improvements, though each can be gamed in its turn. The deeper lesson is that no figure, however refined, can settle what a public needs to know. Metrics can tell editors what readers choose; deciding what deserves to be offered remains a judgement that cannot be handed to the instruments.

passage: A piece of folk wisdom, repeated in many places, holds that a family business rarely survives the founder's grandchildren. The founder builds it through hard work, the children keep it going out of duty, and the grandchildren, raised in comfort, let it slip away. The story is usually told as a lesson about character: wealth softens those who inherit it, and the hunger that built the firm cannot be handed down along with the shares. It is a satisfying story, and like most satisfying stories it is only partly true.

Consider first the plain arithmetic of inheritance. A founder typically owns the whole firm and answers to no one. If the shares are divided among three children, and each of them divides theirs among three more, the third generation may consist of nine or more owners, some of whom work in the business and some of whom have never set foot in it. Those who draw a salary want the profits reinvested; those who live elsewhere want dividends; those who need cash want to sell, and there may be no agreed price at which the others can buy them out. Quarrels follow, but they follow from the structure, and the most energetic cousin in the world could not make them disappear.

A second difficulty lies in how leaders are chosen. A firm that insists the chief executive must be a member of the family has narrowed its field of candidates to a handful of people who happen to share a surname. Even if every one of them is capable, the chance that the best available manager is among them is small. The founder often makes matters worse by postponing the question altogether, because the business is so bound up with his sense of who he is that planning for his own departure feels like planning for his death. When the moment can no longer be avoided, it tends to arrive suddenly, through illness or a quarrel, and the successor is whoever is standing nearest.

None of this means that character is irrelevant; some heirs are indeed less driven than their parents, and some fortunes really are spent rather than lost. But the family firms that last for many generations tend to have one thing in common, and it is not a lucky supply of hard-working grandchildren. They separate the role of owner from the role of manager, write down rules for how shares may be sold within the family, and are willing to hire an outsider to run the business when no relative is suited to it. Their survival is less a triumph of virtue than of design.

passage: Two complaints about digital information circulate side by side, and at first sight they cannot both be true. The first is that the internet never forgets: an embarrassing photograph or an ill-judged remark, once posted, may resurface years later, copied onto sites its author has never heard of. The second is that digital records are alarmingly fragile: web pages vanish, links lead nowhere, and files saved in formats that no current program can read become, for practical purposes, meaningless strings of bits. One might expect a medium to be either durable or perishable, and it is puzzling to hear the same medium accused of both.

The puzzle dissolves once we stop asking about the medium and start asking about copying. A single digital copy is, if anything, more perishable than a sheet of paper. Paper survives neglect; a letter left in a drawer can usually be read a century later by anyone who knows the language. A file left on an old disk depends on the disk surviving, on a machine that can still read the disk, and on software that can still interpret the file, and each of these dependencies decays on its own schedule. What digital information has, and paper largely lacks, is the capacity to be copied perfectly, instantly and at almost no cost. Its persistence therefore depends far less on the durability of any one copy than on whether enough people, or enough systems, have reasons to keep making copies.

Seen in this light, the two complaints describe the same mechanism working on different material. The embarrassing photograph persists because it is the kind of thing people want to pass on, so it is duplicated faster than any single copy can be deleted. The municipal report, the small society's newsletter and the scholar's personal website persist only as long as someone pays for the server and remembers to renew the domain, because few people have any reason to copy them. Nothing about these documents makes them harder to store than the photograph; a newsletter occupies less space than most images. What they lack is a constituency of copiers. When the society disbands or the scholar retires, the single copy that existed sits on a server whose bills no one is paying, and one day it is simply gone, often without anyone noticing that it has happened. Digital persistence, in short, tracks attention and interest rather than value, and the material most likely to vanish is often the unglamorous record that matters most to a historian a generation later.

This suggests that preservation in a digital age is less a technical problem than an institutional one. Better storage media help, but no medium keeps information alive by itself; what keeps it alive is an organisation that has made copying it someone's duty, and that will go on paying for that duty when the material has ceased to be interesting. Libraries and archives have long performed this role for print, and some are trying to perform it for the web. It is tempting to hope that automated tools, which can gather enormous quantities of web pages without human effort, have made such institutions unnecessary. They have not: what such tools gather must still be stored, checked and kept readable as formats change, and someone must decide what deserves that continuing expense. Archives face a difficulty that print archives faced less acutely: the sheer volume of material means that they must choose, and every choice about what to copy is also, in effect, a choice about what to let disappear. The task cannot be avoided by declaring that everything is saved, because what is left to the accidents of attention is saved very unevenly.

passage: Elections are so closely identified with democracy that it can seem perverse to ask whether they are democratic at all. Yet consider what an election rewards. To win, a candidate must stand out from the crowd: be better known, better funded, better connected or simply more persuasive on a platform than the people whose votes are sought. An election is, in this sense, a procedure for picking a distinguished few, and the chambers it fills tend to resemble the electorate less closely than a random sample of that electorate would. Many ancient Greek writers saw the point clearly; for them, filling offices by lot was the characteristically democratic method, and election was a device that favoured the prominent.

The modern case for selection by lot builds on that old intuition. A body drawn at random from the adult population brings into the room the people who are usually spoken about rather than heard: the shift worker, the pensioner, the young parent who would never run for anything. Its members owe nothing to donors or to party managers, since nobody campaigned to put them there. Above all, they are free to change their minds. An elected representative who revises a position after hearing the evidence risks being called a turncoat; a citizen chosen by lot has no platform to betray, and so can treat a question as something to be worked out rather than a position to be defended.

Critics usually reply that ordinary citizens lack the competence to legislate. This objection is weaker than it sounds. Few elected legislators are experts in more than a sliver of what they vote on; they rely on staff, committees and witnesses, and there is no reason a randomly chosen body could not do the same. A more serious difficulty concerns accountability. An elected member who disappoints can be removed at the next election, and the prospect of removal disciplines conduct in between. A member chosen by lot answers to no one, and the very independence that shields such a member from donors also shields him or her from voters. Those who propose replacing elected chambers with lotteries have not, to my mind, answered this objection.

The sensible conclusion is not that lot should displace election but that it can do something election does badly. On some questions elected politicians have every incentive to avoid committing themselves, because any clear answer will cost them votes. A panel chosen at random, given time, evidence and a duty to hear opposing witnesses, can show what ordinary people conclude once they have actually thought the matter through, and its recommendations can then be put to the legislature or to the voters for decision. The lottery's virtue is that it reveals considered public judgement; its limit is that no one has authorised the people it selects to rule.

passage: Special economic zones are usually defended with a simple argument. Where a country's regulations, infrastructure or courts are too poor to attract investors, it may be impossible to repair them everywhere at once; it is easier to draw a boundary around a small area, supply it with reliable power, quick customs clearance and predictable rules, and invite firms to set up inside. The zone becomes a place where the business environment the country cannot yet afford for itself is provided in miniature. Inside the fence, so the thinking goes, investors will find conditions that would take a generation to create outside it.

The reasoning is persuasive within its limits, and it explains why so many governments have tried the experiment. But it also contains the seed of a common failure. A zone designed to protect investors from the surrounding economy can succeed too well. Firms import their components free of duty, assemble them with local labour and export the finished product, while buying almost nothing from domestic suppliers and teaching them nothing. Export figures rise, and an observer counting shipments would call the zone a triumph. Yet the economy outside the fence may be little changed, apart from the wages paid to workers who commute in, and those wages often reflect the kind of routine assembly that is easiest to move elsewhere when costs rise.

What distinguishes the zones that have mattered is not the generosity of their tax holidays but the degree to which they leak. In the more instructive cases, local firms learned to supply the foreign plants, managers trained inside the zone left to start businesses outside it, and, most important, rules first tried within the boundary were later extended across the country once they had shown that they worked. The zone, on this view, is less an enclave than a laboratory, and a laboratory whose findings never leave the building has failed at its central task, whatever it produces.

It would be naive to conclude that governments should simply abolish the boundary and expect the benefits to spread. The isolation of a zone is often what makes it politically possible in the first place, since it lets reformers try new rules without confronting at once every interest that benefits from the old ones. The point is that isolation should be treated as a starting condition to be outgrown, not as the design itself. A zone that is still, after decades, an island of efficiency in an unchanged sea is evidence less of success than of a reform that stalled.

passage: An economy organised entirely by prices would have no need of firms. Every task, from sweeping a floor to designing a circuit, could be bought from whoever offered it most cheaply, and each worker would be a small business selling services by the hour. That actual economies look nothing like this is so familiar that it rarely seems to require explanation. Yet it does. Inside a firm, resources move not because a price has changed but because someone has been told to move them, and the coexistence of these two methods of coordination, the market outside and the hierarchy within, is one of the quieter puzzles of economic life.

The standard answer is that using the market is not free. Before anything can be bought, a buyer must find sellers, compare their terms, write a contract and then check that the contract has been honoured. When a task recurs daily and its details cannot be specified in advance, these costs multiply, and it becomes cheaper to hire someone on open-ended terms and direct the work as it arises. On this view the firm is a device for economising on bargaining: it grows until the cost of organising one more activity internally equals the cost of buying it outside. The account has real explanatory power. It predicts, correctly, that firms tend to bring in-house the activities that are specific to their own operations, where a supplier who knew it was indispensable could hold them to ransom.

What the account leaves out is suggested by its own vocabulary. It describes the firm almost entirely in terms of costs avoided, as if the best a firm could do were to match what an ideal market would have delivered at no expense. But a group of people who work together for years does not merely save on contracts; it produces something that no contract could have bought. Such a group learns which of its members can be trusted with ambiguity, how to divide a problem that none of them fully understands, and which shortcuts are safe. This knowledge is rarely written down and often cannot be, because it lives in habits and in the expectations people hold of one another. It cannot be purchased from outside because it does not exist outside; it is a product of the firm's continued existence.

None of this overturns the bargaining view, which remains the best guide to where the boundary of a firm will fall in any particular case. A carmaker deciding whether to make its own seats is weighing exactly the costs that view describes. The difficulty arises only when the account is taken as a complete theory of what firms are for. Then it makes the firm look like a regrettable necessity, a patch over the imperfections of exchange, and it renders the most valuable thing a firm possesses, the shared competence of people who have learned to work together, invisible to the very analysis that claims to explain it.

passage: One influential account of curiosity holds that it arises from a gap between what a person already knows and what that person would like to know. On this view curiosity is not a general appetite for novelty but a response to a specific, noticed absence: the missing end of a story, the answer to a riddle, the identity of the person who has just telephoned. The account has much to recommend it. It explains why we are rarely curious about subjects of which we know nothing, since we cannot notice a gap in a field we cannot see, and why a little knowledge is often more stimulating than none. It also explains why curiosity so frequently vanishes the moment the answer arrives, leaving behind a satisfaction that is oddly short-lived.

Yet the information gap account fits some cases far better than others. It is at its strongest when the gap is well defined, as in a puzzle with a single solution or a mystery with a culprit. It is weaker when applied to the kind of curiosity that drifts without a target, the impulse that leads someone to wander along the shelves of a library, to turn over stones on a beach or to follow a footnote simply to see where it leads. In these cases there is no specific question waiting to be answered. If anything, the person seeks out situations in which questions might arise, and the pleasure lies as much in the searching as in any particular discovery.

Defenders of the account sometimes reply that the wanderer is simply responding to many small gaps in quick succession. The reply preserves the theory, but at a cost. If any movement of attention whatever can be redescribed after the fact as the closing of a gap, the account no longer explains anything in particular; it becomes a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis. It seems more accurate to say that there are at least two kinds of curiosity, one that seeks to close a specific gap and one that seeks to encounter the unfamiliar, and that the influential account is a good theory of the first.

The distinction matters for anyone who wishes to cultivate curiosity, and for teachers above all. A lesson built on the first kind poses a sharp question and withholds the answer just long enough to make it wanted. A lesson built on the second provides a rich environment and the time to wander in it, without specifying in advance what ought to be found. Both have their place, but a classroom organised entirely around the first may produce students who are excellent at finishing puzzles and rather less inclined to go looking for them.

passage: Few political terms are used as loosely as populism. It is applied to movements of the left and of the right, to leaders who promise to spend lavishly and to those who promise to cut, to campaigns against banks and to campaigns against immigrants. A word that covers so much risks covering nothing, and some scholars have concluded that it is merely a label for whatever kind of politics the speaker happens to dislike. That conclusion is premature. The variety of populist programmes is real, but it may simply show that populism is not a programme at all.

Consider the most common attempt at definition: populism as hostility to elites. This cannot be sufficient, since criticism of the powerful is the ordinary business of opposition in any democracy, and a definition that made every challenger a populist would be useless. What distinguishes the populist is a further claim, namely that there exists a single, authentic people whose will is already known, and that the movement or leader in question alone gives it voice. Opponents are therefore not merely mistaken; they are illegitimate, and citizens who vote for them are not quite part of the people. On this account the core of populism is not anti-elitism but anti-pluralism, a refusal to accept that the people may be divided in good faith.

The value of this definition is that it explains a pattern which approaches based on policy tend to miss. A movement that claims to embody the whole people has difficulty accepting defeat, since a loss at the polls must then be explained as fraud, manipulation or the work of enemies; and once in office it is tempted to treat independent courts, a critical press or a neutral civil service as obstacles placed between the people and its rightful expression. None of this follows from hostility to elites alone. It follows from the claim to a moral monopoly of representation.

Yet the definition carries a hazard of its own. Precisely because it locates the danger in a style of claim rather than in a set of grievances, it can tempt those who use it to dismiss the grievances along with the style. Many people drawn to populist movements have real complaints: about decisions taken far away from them, about parties that seem interchangeable, about institutions that consult them rarely. To treat such voters as a symptom to be managed, rather than as citizens with reasons, is to deny them the standing that pluralism promises, and to confirm the populist story that an elite has stopped listening. The definition is a tool for recognising a threat to democratic competition; it is not a licence to stop asking why the threat finds an audience.

passage: Few claims in social history have travelled as far as the idea that childhood was invented. In its best-known form, put forward in the middle of the twentieth century, it held that medieval Europe had no notion of childhood as a distinct stage of life. Children, on this account, passed almost directly from infancy into the company of adults, working, drinking and dressing as they did; painters showed them as miniature men and women; and parents, facing high infant mortality, refrained from investing much feeling in creatures who might not survive. Childhood as we know it, protected, sentimentalised and set apart, was a discovery of the early modern centuries.

The thesis was a brilliant provocation, and much of it has not survived. Later historians, reading letters, court records, sermons and the evidence of excavated objects, assembled a large body of material showing that medieval parents grieved for dead children, bought or made toys for living ones, and recognised that the young needed particular kinds of care. The argument from paintings proved especially weak. Artistic conventions are not photographs, and an age that painted saints with golden discs around their heads was not simply reporting what it saw. To infer an absence of feeling from an absence of naturalistic portraiture is to mistake a style for a sentiment.

Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that nothing changed. The critics established that medieval people knew children were different and loved them; they did not establish that childhood occupied the same place in social life. What the early modern period did see was the gradual spread of institutions that sorted the young by age and held them apart from adult work: schools divided into classes, a growing literature addressed specifically to children, and eventually laws fixing the ages below which a person could not be employed or married. None of these changes was sudden, and none reached every class or region at once; the children of the poor worked beside adults long after the children of the prosperous had been sent to school. Childhood as a feeling may be ancient. Childhood as a segregated, age-graded stage, organised by institutions, is far more recent.

Seen this way, the original thesis and its critics were partly talking past each other. One side asked whether people recognised and cared for children; the other, without always saying so, asked how societies arranged the passage from birth to adult status. This is why the debate could run for so long without resolution: each side could cite evidence the other did not dispute, because each was answering a different question. The second question is the more fruitful, because it leaves room for the observation that every society has children but not every society has childhood in the same form.

passage: When a town decides to honour someone or something in public, its first instinct is usually to reach for bronze and stone. Durability is treated as a measure of respect: a statue meant to last for centuries seems to say more than a banner meant to last for a week. Yet the history of public art suggests that permanence is less a virtue than a wager, and frequently a losing one. A monument fixes one generation's judgement in a material that will outlast the judgement itself. Within a few decades the figure on the plinth may be unrecognised by most passers-by, and within a century it may be the cause of a quarrel its makers could not have imagined.

The problem is not that later generations are fickle. It is that a permanent work is designed to end discussion rather than to take part in it. Once installed, it asks only to be accepted; there is no procedure built into it for being reconsidered. When disagreement finally arrives, it therefore arrives as a crisis, with petitions, counter-petitions and arguments over whether removal amounts to erasing history. A city that had expected its public art to change would face no such crisis, because it would already possess a habit of revisiting what stands in its squares.

Temporary works offer one way of building that habit. A plinth that hosts a different commission every year or two, a sculpture placed in a park for a single season, a mural painted on the understanding that it will be painted over: each of these makes public art an occasion rather than a verdict. People argue about the new piece, grow fond of it or feel relieved to see it go, and in doing so they practise exactly the kind of collective judgement that a permanent statue forecloses. The work matters less as an object than as the conversation it starts.

This argument has limits, and they should be stated. Temporary art can slide into novelty for its own sake, a rotating series of spectacles chosen to attract visitors rather than to say anything. And some public works aim at permanence for good reason: a memorial to the dead of a war or a disaster is meant to resist the passing of time, because forgetting is precisely the danger it guards against. The case against bronze is not a case against all lasting memorials. It is a case against the assumption that whatever a public wishes to honour must be honoured in a form that can never be questioned without a fight.

passage: A parent who hears a child begin a sentence in one language and finish it in another often worries that the child has learned neither properly. Teachers have voiced the same anxiety, and so, at times, have bilingual speakers themselves, who describe their own mixing with a kind of apology, as though it betrayed a laziness they ought to overcome. The assumption behind the worry is simple: a speaker who switches must be reaching for a word he does not have, and a speaker who is constantly reaching has not finished learning.

The assumption is not absurd, and sometimes it is true. Anyone who has lived between two languages knows the moment when the word for a kitchen utensil, or for a form at the bank, has been acquired in one language and simply not in the other. But careful recordings of bilingual conversation suggest that such gaps account for only part of what happens, and not the most interesting part. Switches tend to fall at points where the grammars of the two languages fit together and to avoid points where they clash, so that a sentence begun in one language and finished in another is usually well formed by the standards of both. A speaker who was merely groping for words would not be so tidy. To switch in this way, one needs to know two grammars well enough to sense, without thinking, where they can be joined.

Nor is the timing of a switch random. Speakers move into the other language to report what someone else said, to mark a change of topic, to soften a refusal, to signal that a remark is a joke, or to draw a listener in or shut one out. A grandmother's proverb may be quoted in the language she used, not because the speaker cannot translate it, but because the translation would lose the grandmother. In such uses the switch itself carries meaning, much as a change of tone does within a single language; it is a resource that monolingual speakers lack, not a failure that they have avoided.

None of this means that every setting must welcome mixing. An examination set in one language, or a document that must be read by people who know only one, may reasonably require a speaker to stay within it, and a bilingual who could not do so would indeed have a problem. The error lies in treating the ability to keep languages apart as the measure of competence, and the habit of combining them as its absence. Most bilinguals can do both. Judging them by the first alone is like judging a pianist only by whether she can play with one hand.

passage: Many people who would never tell a lie are perfectly comfortable misleading. Asked whether he has finished a report, an employee replies that he has been working on it all morning, which is true, and which he says precisely so that his manager will conclude that the report is nearly done. He has not lied, he tells himself; if his manager draws the wrong conclusion, that is her inference, not his assertion. The intuition behind this self-defence is widely shared, and it is not merely self-serving. Ordinary moral thinking, many legal systems and a long tradition of moral reasoning have treated the outright falsehood as a graver matter than the true statement artfully deployed.

Yet when we ask what is wrong with lying in the first place, the distinction begins to look thin. The harm of a lie consists chiefly in two things: the listener ends up with a false belief that he did not choose, and the trust he extended to the speaker has been turned against him. Both harms are present in the case of the employee. His manager now believes something false about the report, and she believes it because she assumed, reasonably, that a colleague answering her question was trying to answer it. The employee exploited exactly that assumption. That he did so by selecting true words rather than inventing false ones changes the technique, not the result.

There is, however, one setting in which the distinction earns its keep. In a negotiation over the price of a used car, both parties know that the other is pursuing its own advantage, and each is expected to read the other's statements with suspicion. A seller who says that several people have asked about the car, when several have indeed asked but none has made an offer, leaves the buyer free to discount the remark, and a competent buyer will. Where the listener is on guard by convention, the responsibility for drawing inferences is genuinely shared, and the misleader has exploited much less trust than the liar, who asserts something false that even a wary listener has no means of checking.

What this suggests is that the moral line runs less between lying and misleading than between relationships in which listeners are entitled to rely on a speaker's cooperation and those in which they are not. In the first kind, which includes most of our dealings with doctors, colleagues, friends and family, the careful choice of true but misleading words offers almost no moral shelter. In the second, it offers some. The employee who congratulates himself on never having lied has simply mistaken the setting he is in.

passage: Ask people what grief involves and many will describe a sequence: denial, then anger, then bargaining, then depression, and at last acceptance. The sequence has become so familiar that it can seem like a discovery about human nature, as settled as the stages of a fever. It began, however, as a description of how some terminally ill patients responded to the news of their own approaching death, drawn from clinical conversations rather than from any systematic study of the bereaved. Its migration from the dying to the grieving, and from a set of observations to something closer to a timetable, happened largely outside the kind of research that might have tested it.

When grief has been studied directly, the tidy sequence has not fared well. Bereaved people commonly report several of the named feelings at once, or in no particular order, and many report some of them hardly at all. Perhaps the most striking finding is how many people cope with a loss far better than the model would lead one to expect, experiencing intense sorrow that gradually eases over months without passing through anything resembling distinct stages. Resilience of this kind is not denial in disguise; for a good number of people it seems simply to be the ordinary course that grief takes.

The harm of the model lies less in its inaccuracy than in what people do with it. A description of what some people feel becomes a standard of what everyone ought to feel, and departures from the standard begin to look like problems requiring attention. The widow who is not angry may be told that she has not yet faced her loss; the son who feels relief after a parent's long illness may wonder what is wrong with him. Friends, and even professionals, may wait for a stage that never arrives, or press a grieving person to move on to the next one as though grief were a course with a syllabus.

It would be unfair, though, to treat the model's popularity as mere credulity. It arrived at a time when dying and grief were seldom spoken of openly, and it gave people words for feelings, anger above all, that they might otherwise have hidden or been ashamed of. That was a real service, and it should not be forgotten in the rush to correct the record. The task now is to keep what the model offered, the permission to feel a wide range of things, while dropping the suggestion that those feelings must arrive in a fixed order, or arrive at all.

passage: Few observations seem less in need of explanation than the darkness of the night sky. The sun sets and the heavens go dark; what else would they do? Yet for several centuries astronomers who took seriously the idea of an infinite, unchanging cosmos found that darkness genuinely puzzling, and their reasoning deserves to be reconstructed, because its premises once seemed almost beyond question. Suppose that stars are scattered more or less uniformly through boundless space. Then any direction in which an observer looks, pursued far enough, must sooner or later meet the bright disc of a star. Remote stars certainly look dimmer than nearby ones, but the number of stars at each successive distance grows in step with the dimming, so that every shell of space contributes as much light as the one inside it. On these assumptions the heavens should glow in all directions with the brilliance of the solar surface.

The first replies tried to rescue the infinite universe by blocking the light. Perhaps clouds of dust between the stars absorbed the glow of the most distant ones. The suggestion sounds reasonable until one follows it through, for dust that absorbs light for long enough is warmed by it, and eventually it glows as brightly as the light it swallows. Over an unlimited span of time, absorption delays the problem; it does not remove it. Other proposals arranged the stars in clusters within clusters, so that lines of sight could slip between them, but these seemed contrived, a geometry invented to answer a single awkward question.

The resolution now accepted is both simpler and stranger. The universe we can observe has a finite age, and light, however swift, needs time to cross space. Most directions therefore never terminate on a star, because the glow of sufficiently remote stars is still in transit, and to look far enough out is to look back to an epoch before any stars had formed. The expansion of space contributes a second effect, stretching the light of faraway sources to longer and feebler wavelengths. Neither point needs to be accepted merely because it dissolves the paradox; each is supported by independent lines of evidence gathered long after the puzzle was first posed.

It would be an exaggeration to say that the darkness of the night proves that the universe had a beginning. Taken alone, it rules out only one combination of assumptions, namely that space is infinite, evenly stocked with stars and unchanging forever, but that is no small thing. A fact available to anyone who steps outside after sunset turns out to be incompatible with what was, for a long time, the most natural picture of the cosmos. The lesson is less about stars than about observation, for the most ordinary features of experience are not always the least informative; sometimes they seem ordinary only because we have stopped asking why they are as they are.

passage: A library catalogue looks like the least ideological of documents. Its function, apparently, is merely to inform a reader where a particular book is located, and the call number on a spine seems as neutral as a street address. But a classification scheme does more than locate. To place a book, it must first decide what the book is about, and to do that it must divide the whole of knowledge into classes, arrange the classes in an order, and decide which subjects deserve broad territory and which can be squeezed into a corner. Every call number is, in compressed form, a small theory of what its book is about. These are not merely technical decisions. They are judgments about how the world is organised, made by particular people at a particular time, and then built, quite literally, into buildings.

The judgments show most clearly where a scheme meets subjects its makers did not think central. One widely used decimal scheme, devised in the nineteenth century, gave most of the numbers in its religion class to varieties of Christianity, leaving the rest of the world's traditions to share a small remainder. Nobody needs to suppose malice to explain this; the scheme reflected the collections and the assumptions of the libraries its maker knew. But the consequence outlived the assumptions. A library using such a scheme in a city of many faiths must either cram large collections into long, unwieldy numbers or improvise local fixes that make its shelves harder to share with other libraries.

The effect is not confined to how much space a subject receives. Classification also governs adjacency, and adjacency governs discovery. A reader who goes to the shelf for one book finds its neighbours, and much of what people learn in libraries they learn through this kind of sideways encounter. Suppose a hypothetical study of household labour is shelved among works on economics; its browsers will meet it as an argument about production and value. Shelved instead among works on the family, it will be met as an argument about domestic life. The book is the same, but the conversation it is placed in is not, and the scheme, rather than the author, has chosen the conversation.

From this one might conclude that classification is a kind of censorship which libraries should abandon in favour of keyword search, which appears to impose no order at all. The conclusion does not follow. Search systems rank their results, and ranking embodies choices just as surely as shelving does; the choices are merely harder to see. Moreover, a collection with no arrangement is not neutral but unusable, since a reader can then find only what she already knows to ask for, whereas the browser of a well-ordered shelf may stumble on books she never knew existed. Some order is the price of a library's being useful, and every order has a point of view.

The more defensible lesson is that classification should be treated as revisable and should be visible as a choice. Schemes have in fact been revised many times, often after communities pointed out how they were misdescribed, and catalogues increasingly allow a book to carry several subject headings even though it can stand in only one place. Revision is not a confession of failure but the ordinary condition of any scheme that tries to describe a body of knowledge which keeps changing beneath it. No scheme will ever be neutral. What can reasonably be asked of one is that it knows it is not, and that it leaves room for readers to cross the boundaries it draws.

options.B: the collections and assumptions of the libraries that were familiar to the person who devised the scheme.

options.D: the technical limits of decimal notation, which could not divide a single class into more than a few parts.

passage: When people imagine an intelligent animal, they usually imagine something built on the plan of their own bodies: a large brain in the head that gathers information, makes decisions and issues commands to obedient limbs. The octopus is a standing challenge to that picture. Its evolutionary line separated from ours more than half a billion years ago, long before either lineage had anything resembling a complex brain, so whatever intelligence it now has was assembled independently. And it was assembled on a strikingly different plan, for more of the octopus's neurons lie in its arms than in its central brain.

The arrangement has consequences that can be observed. An octopus arm can carry out a sequence of movements, such as reaching towards an object and bending to draw it in, with little apparent direction from the centre, and an arm separated from the body will for a time continue to respond to touch and to grasp what it meets. Each arm, it seems, handles much of the detail of its own movement, while the central brain sets broader goals. Instead of a commander and its troops, the better image might be a coordinator working with partners that each know their own business.

Popular writing has been quick to turn this into a slogan, describing the octopus as an animal with nine brains, or as a colony of minds sharing one body. The slogan goes too far. The arms are not independent agents with purposes of their own; they share a body, a nervous system and, in ordinary life, a single course of action, and the animal behaves as one creature pursuing one end at a time. What the anatomy shows is not that the octopus is many minds but that one mind can be organised so that much of its work is done at the edges.

That is the real lesson, and it reaches beyond octopuses. Much thinking about intelligence, in animals and in machines alike, has assumed that it must be centralised: that there must be some single place where everything comes together and is decided. The octopus suggests that centralisation is one solution among several, suited to some bodies and not to others. An animal with eight flexible arms and no skeleton faces a control problem that no single centre could easily solve, since each arm can bend at any point along its length and in any direction. Handing much of the work to the arms may be less an evolutionary curiosity than a sensible answer to the body the animal actually has.

passage: For a long time economists were embarrassed by a simple question. Water is essential to life and diamonds are not, yet water is cheap and diamonds are dear; how could prices, which were supposed to reflect value, so plainly invert the order of importance? Eighteenth-century writers posed the puzzle as a contrast between value in use and value in exchange, and many concluded that exchange value must therefore have some source other than usefulness. The most influential answer located that source in the costs of production, and above all in labour: diamonds are dear because finding and cutting them takes enormous effort, while water, in most places, merely has to be collected.

The cost theory had obvious merits, since goods that are hard to produce are frequently expensive, but it struggled with cases in which effort and price come apart. A pearl found by chance in an oyster served at dinner fetches no less than one obtained by days of diving, and a wine from a celebrated year commands its price long after the labour that made it has been forgotten. The resolution that eventually prevailed, worked out independently by several writers in the later nineteenth century, abandoned the attempt to attach value to goods as such. What matters, it held, is not the usefulness of water in general but the usefulness of one more unit of it to someone who already has a certain amount. A person with enough water to drink, cook and wash would gain little from an extra bucket, while a person with few diamonds, or none, would prize one more highly. Price tracks this marginal usefulness, not the total.

The resolution is genuine, and its elegance is rightly admired. But it achieved both more than it is usually credited with and less. It achieved more because it moved value from things to situations: the same bucket of water is nearly worthless in a town beside a river and beyond price to a traveller lost in a desert, although nothing about the water has changed. It achieved less because it was never a theory of importance. To say that water is cheap is to say that, where it is plentiful, nobody would give much for one more unit of it; it is not to say that water matters little. The marginal account explains why prices may be low on goods that are indispensable, and in doing so it warns us against reading prices as a ranking of what matters.

That warning is regularly forgotten. Public argument often treats the market price of something as the measure of its contribution, so that an activity commanding high prices is assumed to be more valuable to society than one commanding low ones, and resources that cost nothing, such as clean air, are treated as though they were of no account until they become scarce. The marginal theory does not license this inference; if anything it predicts the error, since it shows that abundance alone can drive a price towards zero whatever the total importance of the good. Abundance, moreover, is not always permanent, and a price set while a resource was plentiful says little about what it will be worth once it is not.

None of this is a case against prices, which remain an unrivalled means of coordinating what millions of people do with information that no single mind possesses. It is a case for remembering what question a price answers. A price tells us what one more unit of something is worth to those at the margin, here and now. It does not tell us what the whole of it is worth, or what it would be worth to people who are not in the market at all, and a society that forgets the difference may discover the value of its cheapest goods only when it is too late to pay for them.

passage: The laws of war rest on a premise that, stated baldly, can seem scandalous. A soldier who fights for an aggressor and a soldier who fights to repel him are held to have exactly the same rights on the battlefield: each may lawfully kill enemy combatants, each must spare civilians and prisoners, and neither commits a crime merely by taking part. Whether the war itself was just, a question settled, if at all, by the cause for which it was begun, is treated as irrelevant to how it may be fought. The justice of going to war and justice in the conduct of war are kept in separate compartments, and the ordinary soldier is answerable only for the second.

Philosophical critics have pressed hard on this separation, and their central argument is difficult to resist. Outside war, we do not think that someone who attacks without justification acquires a right to kill those who resist him; a robber who is fired on by the guard he is trying to overpower may not shoot back and call it self-defence. Why should the matter change when the attacker wears a uniform and acts on orders? If the right to kill in war derives, as it must, from the right to defend against an unjust threat, then those who pose the unjust threat seem to have no such right at all. On this view, the soldier of an aggressor state who kills a defending soldier does wrong, however scrupulously he observes the rules of conduct.

I think the critics are right about the underlying morality and wrong about what follows for the laws of war. Rules for the conduct of hostilities must be followed by people who are frightened, poorly informed and dependent on their own government's account of why they are fighting. Nearly every belligerent believes, or is told, that its cause is just. A rule that granted the right to kill only to soldiers on the just side would therefore be claimed by both sides, and would offer no restraint precisely where restraint is most needed; worse, it would invite each side to treat captured enemies as criminals rather than as prisoners. The symmetry of the laws of war is not a judgement that both sides are equally innocent. It is a convention adopted because the alternative would make war more savage without making it more just.

Conceding this does not license the conclusion that soldiers bear no responsibility for the wars they fight. A convention that withholds legal blame is not a certificate of moral innocence, and there will be wars whose injustice is so plain that an ordinary soldier could see it and ought to refuse. The doctrine of equality is best understood not as a truth about the morality of killing but as a practical arrangement that we maintain, knowingly, because it does more to limit the horror of war than any rule that tracked the moral truth more closely could do.

passage: Most people who hold opinions about celebrated modern buildings have never been inside them. They know them from photographs, and the photographs share a family resemblance. They are taken in the weeks after completion, before the occupants have moved in, on a day chosen for its light. Furniture, if there is any, is placed by the photographer; people, if they appear at all, are small and blurred, present to give scale rather than to show use. The building is caught at the single moment when it most resembles its architect's intention and least resembles the place it will become.

There is nothing sinister in this. The photographer is paid to show the work at its best, as a portrait painter is, and an empty room displays its proportions more clearly than a crowded one. The difficulty lies in what happens when such images become the principal medium through which architecture is judged. Reputations are made in magazines and, increasingly, on screens, and they are made quickly, long before anyone knows whether the roof leaks, whether the offices overheat in summer, or whether the grand atrium is a pleasure to cross on a wet Monday morning. Critics, who seldom have the time or the budget to return, write from the same images, and the first account of a building tends to become the account that is repeated. A building's reputation is thus fixed at the very moment when least is known about it.

The effect is not confined to critics. Architects are not naive about how their work will be seen, and a profession whose rewards follow the photograph will tend, without anyone deciding it, to design for the photograph. Qualities that register in a single frame, a dramatic cantilever, a pure white surface, a striking silhouette against the sky, come to be favoured over qualities that can be experienced only over time or through the other senses: the way a staircase feels under tired feet, the acoustics of a dining room, the dignity with which a material ages. White render photographs beautifully and often weathers badly; a brick that looks dull on the day of opening may look better in its fiftieth year than in its first.

Defenders of the photograph reply that it is the only way most of us can see buildings in distant cities, and that the alternative, judging only what one has personally visited, would make criticism parochial. They add that many buildings which photograph well also work well, and that architects idealised their work in drawings long before the camera existed. Each of these points is fair, yet none of them reaches the central point. The complaint is not that photographs flatter, which drawings did too, but that the moment of photographing has become the moment of judgement, and that the qualities a photograph can register have quietly become the qualities that count.

One modest remedy would be to make the second look as normal as the first. A building photographed and discussed again after ten years of use, with its occupants in it and its materials weathered, would be judged on evidence that the opening day cannot supply. Such a practice would not abolish the glamour of the new, and it is not meant to. It would simply give the slower virtues of a building a chance to be seen by those who will never walk through it, and it would give architects a reason to care about the tenth year as much as the first, since that is when they would next be judged.

passage: For a long time emotions were cast as the adversaries of reason, surges of feeling that cloud judgement and must be governed by it. A more recent and considerably more flattering view inverts this picture. Emotions, it holds, are themselves judgements, or are at least constructed around them. To be afraid of a dog is to judge that the dog is dangerous; to feel indignant is to regard oneself as having been treated unjustly. The view has an obvious appeal. It explains why emotions can be appropriate or inappropriate to their circumstances, why we can sometimes argue a friend out of her jealousy by showing her that she has misread a situation, and why emotions are directed at objects rather than being mere sensations, like an itch or a cramp, that are about nothing at all.

The difficulty arises from emotions that persist against judgement. A traveller may know perfectly well that flying is far safer than the drive to the airport, may say so and sincerely believe it, and still grip the armrest in terror as the aircraft climbs. If fear were a judgement that flying is dangerous, the traveller would be simultaneously affirming and denying the same proposition, and her condition would be a straightforward contradiction. Yet it does not feel like a contradiction, nor do we treat it as one; we recognise it as a familiar kind of inner conflict, unpleasant but not absurd.

A better model is perception. When two lines of equal length are drawn with arrowheads pointing in opposite directions, one continues to look longer even after a ruler has shown that they are equal. Seeing is not believing, so the conflict involves no contradiction. Emotions, on this model, are something like perceptions of value: fear presents the climbing aircraft as dangerous in the way the illusion presents one line as longer. Such presentations are usually reliable and usually agree with our considered views, which is why the judgement theory seemed so plausible. When they disagree, we have the emotional counterpart of an optical illusion.

The analogy should not be pressed too far. We do not blame anyone for seeing the lines as unequal, but we do sometimes criticise people for their fears and resentments, and we expect them to work on them. This suggests that emotions, unlike most perceptions, are partly answerable to the person who has them: they can be reshaped over time through reflection and repeated experience, even if they cannot be dismissed by a single act of judgement. The perceptual model explains why emotional conflict is not contradiction; it must be supplemented to explain why it is nevertheless an occasion for responsibility.
